subject: CREATIVE ARTS
title: Descant Recorder
overview: The descant recorder is a small wind instrument played with the mouth and the fingers. In this sub-strand you will name its parts, learn how to keep it clean and store it safely, and play the notes B, A and G with a good posture and a gentle breath. You will then play simple tunes on those three notes and listen to one another.

lessons.title: Parts of the descant recorder
objectives: Name the head joint, middle joint, foot joint and finger holes.
Assemble the recorder so the holes line up.
Hold it the right way up before any playing.
lessons.intro: A descant recorder looks like one tube, but it comes apart into pieces. If you do not know which piece is which, you cannot put it together or find the notes.
lessons.notes:
The descant recorder is the small recorder most schools use. It is sometimes called a soprano recorder. Sound is made by blowing gently into the mouthpiece while fingers cover and uncover holes. Covering more holes makes a lower note.

### The three joints
- The **head joint** is the top piece. It has the **beak** (the mouthpiece you rest on your lips) and the **window**, a rectangular opening underneath where the air splits and the sound begins.
- The **middle joint** is the long middle piece. Most of the finger holes are on it.
- The **foot joint** is the small bottom piece. It has the last hole, often a double hole.

### Finger holes
The holes on the front are covered by the fingers. The hole at the back of the head joint, or at the top of the middle joint depending on the model, is covered by the left thumb. You do not need every hole yet. Notes B, A and G use only the left thumb and the first fingers of the left hand. The other holes still have to be there, and you must not block them by mistake.

### Putting it together
Fit the foot joint onto the middle joint, then fit the head joint. Use a gentle twist. Do not force the pieces or bang them on a desk. The window of the head joint should line up with the finger holes. If the head joint faces sideways, your fingers will not sit on the holes.

Left hand goes at the top, nearer the beak. Right hand goes at the bottom. If you swap hands, the notes B, A and G will not work. Look at a chart or a real recorder and touch each part as you name it. Familiarity means you can name the parts without looking at a label.

keyWords.meaning: a small recorder played by blowing and covering finger holes
the top piece with the beak and the window
the long piece with most of the finger holes
the small bottom piece
an opening covered by a finger to change the note

examples.problem: Which joint has the beak and the window?
steps: The mouthpiece is at the top.
The top piece is the head joint.

examples.problem: A learner puts the right hand at the top. What will go wrong?
steps: The left hand must be nearer the beak.
Notes B, A and G use the left-hand fingers.
examples.answer: The fingers will be on the wrong holes, so B, A and G will not sound correctly.

activity.title: Name and assemble
materials: A descant recorder for each player or for each pair
A diagram or Baroque fingering chart
steps: Take the recorder apart carefully.
Point to the head joint, middle joint, foot joint, beak, window and finger holes.
Assemble it with a gentle twist so the window lines up with the holes.
Place the left hand at the top and the right hand below, without playing yet.
Your partner checks the lineup and the hands.

practice.question: Name the three joints of a descant recorder from top to bottom.
practice.answer: Head joint, middle joint, foot joint.

practice.question: What is the window?
practice.answer: The rectangular opening where the air splits and the sound begins.

practice.question: Which hand goes nearer the beak?
practice.answer: The left hand.

summary: The recorder has a head joint, a middle joint and a foot joint.
Finger holes change the notes.
Assemble it gently, with the left hand at the top.

lessons.title: Caring for the recorder
objectives: Clean and store a descant recorder correctly.
Explain how hygiene stops germs spreading.
Give two reasons why care makes the instrument last.
lessons.intro: A recorder goes in the mouth, so it is not like a drum that the whole class can hit in turn. How you clean it, hold it and put it away decides both its life and the health of the class.
lessons.notes:
Care has two aims. Hygiene keeps germs from spreading. Gentle handling and storage make the recorder last. Lasting a long time is what longevity means.

### Hygiene
- Play only your own recorder. Do not lend the beak to a friend “just to try”.
- Wash your hands before you play.
- Do not play if you have a mouth infection, and do not share mouthpieces when someone has a cold or a cough. This helps prevent communicable diseases, the illnesses that pass from person to person.
- After playing, shake moisture out of the head joint. Wipe the beak.
- A plastic school recorder may be washed in lukewarm soapy water, rinsed and dried. Do not use boiling water. Do not leave it to soak all day.
- If your recorder is wooden, do not soak it. Wipe it and let it dry. Ask the teacher before washing any recorder that is not plastic.

### Handling
- Do not bite the beak.
- Do not bang the joints together or use the recorder as a pointer.
- Twist gently when you take it apart. Forcing a stuck joint can crack it.
- Carry it in your hand or case, not in a pocket full of pens.

### Storage
- Dry it before you put it away.
- Keep it in a case or a clean bag.
- Do not leave it in hot sun or on a window sill. Heat can warp plastic and crack wood.
- Store it where it will not be sat on.

A dirty, shared, sun-baked recorder becomes unpleasant to play and may not sound. A clean, personal, cool, dry recorder is ready for the next lesson.

keyWords.meaning: clean habits that stop germs spreading
a long life; here, the recorder lasting a long time
an illness that can pass from one person to another

examples.problem: Two learners have a cold and want to try each other’s recorders. Why is that a poor idea?
steps: Colds spread through shared mouthpieces.
Each player should use only their own recorder.
examples.answer: They could pass germs to each other. Each person should play only their own recorder.

examples.problem: A plastic recorder was left on a hot window sill. What risk is that?
steps: Heat can bend plastic.
examples.answer: The recorder may warp, so the joints and holes no longer fit well.

activity.title: Clean, dry and store
materials: Lukewarm soapy water if the teacher says the recorder is plastic
steps: In a group, list ways of caring for the recorder and why each one matters.
Wash hands. If the recorder is plastic and the teacher agrees, wash it in lukewarm soapy water and rinse it.
Dry the joints and the beak.
Assemble it gently, then take it apart again and put it in the case.
Agree one class rule: nobody shares a mouthpiece.

practice.question: Why should learners not share recorder mouthpieces?
practice.answer: Germs that cause communicable diseases can spread from mouth to mouth.

practice.question: What water is safe for a plastic recorder?
practice.answer: Lukewarm soapy water, followed by a rinse and drying. Not boiling water.

practice.question: Give two storage rules.
practice.answer: Any two: dry it first, use a case or clean bag, keep it out of hot sun, do not leave it where it can be sat on.

summary: Play only your own recorder and wash your hands.
Wash a plastic recorder in lukewarm water, then dry it.
Store it cool, dry and protected so it lasts.

lessons.title: Posture and how to hold the recorder
objectives: Sit or stand with a playing posture.
Place the left hand on top and seal the holes with the pads of the fingers.
Support the recorder with the right hand without covering holes you do not need.
lessons.intro: A hunched back and flat fingers make the recorder squeak before the tune has started. Posture is the first playing technique.
lessons.notes:
Posture means the way you sit or stand and the way you hold the instrument. A good posture lets the breath move and lets the fingers seal the holes.

### Body
- Sit toward the front of the chair, or stand with both feet on the ground.
- Keep the back tall, not stiff. The shoulders stay down.
- The head is level. Do not tuck the chin hard into the chest.
- Hold the recorder at a slant, pointing down and slightly forward, about halfway between straight up and straight out. It should not point at the floor between your feet, and it should not stick straight out like a stick.

### Hands
- Left hand on top. The left thumb covers the thumb hole at the back.
- The pads of the fingers, not the very tips and not the flat middle of the finger, cover the holes.
- Fingers are curved, as if each hand is holding a small ball.
- Right hand supports the lower joint. For notes B, A and G the right-hand fingers stay just above their holes, ready, but they do not cover them.
- Elbows hang relaxed. Do not glue them to your ribs and do not flap them out.

### A seal test
Cover one hole and ask a partner to look around the finger. If they can see the hole, air will leak and the note will be wrong or noisy. Leaks are the main reason beginners think the recorder is broken.

Practise the holding shape in silence. Lifting and replacing one finger without looking at the hole is the skill you will need when the notes arrive. Keep the recorder out of your mouth until the next lesson, so that posture is learnt before blowing.

keyWords.meaning: the way you sit or stand and hold the instrument
the soft front of the fingertip that seals a hole
to cover a hole completely so air cannot leak

examples.problem: A learner’s note will not sound and a partner can see half of hole 1. What is the cause?
steps: A visible hole means air is leaking.
The pad of the finger must seal it.
examples.answer: The finger is not sealing the hole.

examples.problem: Which hand is on top when playing B, A and G?
steps: Those notes use the upper holes.
The left hand plays the upper holes.

activity.title: Silent holding practice
steps: Sit or stand tall and hold the recorder at a comfortable downward slant.
Place the left thumb and fingers in a curved shape. The right hand supports the bottom.
Your partner checks that the left hand is on top and that covered holes are fully sealed.
Lift one finger and replace it five times without twisting the recorder.
Rest the recorder in your lap or case. Nobody blows yet.

practice.question: Where should the left hand be?
practice.answer: At the top, nearer the beak.

practice.question: Which part of the finger seals a hole?
practice.answer: The pad of the finger.

practice.question: What does the right hand do while you play B, A and G?
practice.answer: It supports the lower part of the recorder and stays ready, without covering holes.

summary: Sit or stand tall, with the recorder slanting gently downward.
Left hand on top, fingers curved, holes sealed.
The right hand supports the instrument for these three notes.

lessons.title: Blowing and a good tone
objectives: Start a sound with the tongue.
Use a gentle, steady breath.
Explain what causes a squeak.
lessons.intro: The recorder does not need the huge breath you use to blow up a ball. It needs a small, steady stream of air, started neatly with the tongue.
lessons.notes:
Tone is the quality of the sound: clear, gentle and steady, or squeaky, breathy and harsh. The question for this instrument is how a good tone is produced.

### The mouth
Rest the beak on the lower lip and close the lips gently around it. Do not bite. Only a small part of the beak goes into the mouth. The teeth do not clamp down. The cheeks stay flat, not puffed out.

### The tongue
Start each note by saying “doo” or “too” inside the mouth. The tongue touches the back of the upper teeth and comes away as the air begins. This is called tonguing. It makes a clean start. Blowing without the tongue makes a fuzzy “whoosh”.

### The breath
Blow warm, slow air, as if you were steaming a mirror. If you blow hard, the recorder jumps to a high squeak. If you blow too little, you get a whisper and no note. Steady air in the middle is the tone you want.

### A first sound
Cover no front holes. Cover the thumb hole only if your teacher’s chart asks for that first open note. Many classes first practise a gentle tongued sound so the ears learn a clear tone before the fingers complicate it. If the sound squeaks:

- blow more gently
- check that you are not biting
- check for leaking fingers if any holes are covered
- check that the head joint window is lined up and not blocked by dirt

Stop every few minutes and let moisture out of the head joint. A blocked window gurgles. Good tone is gentle air, a tongued start, a sealed hole and a clear window.

keyWords.meaning: the quality of the sound
starting a note with the tongue, as in “doo” or “too”
a high unwanted sound caused by blowing too hard or by a leak

examples.problem: Every note jumps to a high squeak. What should the player change first?
steps: Hard blowing makes the recorder overblow.
The breath should be gentle and steady.
examples.answer: Blow more gently, with warm steady air.

examples.problem: The sound starts with a fuzzy whoosh. Which technique is missing?
steps: A clean start uses the tongue.
Saying “doo” or “too” is tonguing.

activity.title: Gentle “doo” sounds
steps: Check posture and a clean beak.
Practise saying “doo doo doo doo” on a gentle breath, four sounds, then rest.
If the sound squeaks, soften the breath and try again.
A partner says whether the tone was clear or forced.
Shake moisture out and rest the recorder.

practice.question: How can a good tone be produced on the descant recorder?
practice.answer: Use a gentle steady breath, start the note with the tongue, seal the holes, and keep the window clear.

practice.question: What happens if you blow too hard?
practice.answer: The note squeaks or jumps too high.

practice.question: Should you bite the beak?
practice.answer: No. The lips rest gently around it.

summary: Lips rest gently on the beak. Do not bite or puff the cheeks.
Start notes with “doo” or “too”.
A gentle steady breath makes a clear tone.

lessons.title: Playing the note B
objectives: Finger note B on a Baroque descant recorder.
Play four steady B notes with a clear tone.
Fix a leak or a squeak on B.
lessons.intro: B is the first of the three notes in this sub-strand. It uses the fewest fingers, so it is the best place to join posture, breath and a sealed hole.
lessons.notes:
Use a Baroque fingering chart, the chart used with school descant recorders in this design. For note B, only two holes are covered:

- the left thumb covers the thumb hole at the back
- the left index finger covers hole 1, the first hole on the front

All the other holes stay open. The right hand still supports the recorder.

### Steps
1. Sit or stand tall. Left hand on top.
2. Seal the thumb hole and hole 1. Look once to check, then look forward.
3. Start with “doo” and a gentle breath.
4. Hold the note while you count “one”, then stop the air with the tongue.
5. Play four separate B notes: doo, doo, doo, doo. Keep them the same length.

### If B will not sound
- The index finger is leaking. Seal with the pad.
- The thumb is only half on the hole.
- You are blowing too hard.
- You swapped hands.
- The head joint has twisted so the window is no longer in line.

Watch a live demonstration or a recording if the teacher provides one. Copy the fingers, not the volume. A recording that is loud does not mean you should blast.

When four notes are clean, play four slow B notes and four quicker ones. The note name stays B. Only the rhythm changes. Rest often so you do not become dizzy. Wipe the beak before you put the recorder down.

keyWords.meaning: the note played with the left thumb and the first finger only
the standard fingering system used on many school descant recorders

examples.problem: Which fingers cover holes for note B?
steps: Thumb at the back.
Index finger on the first front hole.
No other fingers.
examples.answer: The left thumb and the left index finger.

examples.problem: A player covers thumb, hole 1 and hole 2, and expects B. Which note are they fingering instead?
steps: B is thumb and hole 1 only.
Adding hole 2 changes the note to A.

activity.title: Four clean B notes
materials: A recording or teacher demonstration if available
steps: Watch the demonstration of note B.
Finger B in silence and ask a partner to check thumb and index finger.
Play four slow tongued B notes.
Repair leaks or squeaks using the checklist.
Play four B notes again and put the recorder down to dry.

practice.question: How do you finger note B?
practice.answer: Cover the left thumb hole and the first front hole only.

practice.question: How many separate B notes are in a practice of four notes?
Give two reasons a B might squeak or fail.
practice.answer: Any two: leaking finger, thumb half covering, blowing too hard, hands swapped, head joint twisted.

summary: B uses the left thumb and the index finger only.
Tongue four steady notes with a gentle breath.
Seal the holes and keep the window lined up.

lessons.title: Playing the notes A and G
objectives: Finger A and G correctly.
Move from B to A to G without twisting the recorder.
Hear that G is the lowest of the three notes.
lessons.intro: Each new covered hole lowers the note. A adds one finger to B. G adds one more finger to A. The breath and the posture stay the same.
lessons.notes:
Keep the left hand on top and the thumb sealed for all three notes.

### Note A
Cover the thumb hole, hole 1 and hole 2. Hole 2 is closed by the left middle finger. Hole 3 and the right-hand holes stay open. Play four tongued A notes. They should sound a step lower than B.

### Note G
Cover the thumb hole, hole 1, hole 2 and hole 3. Hole 3 is closed by the left ring finger. Play four tongued G notes. G is the lowest of these three notes. If G comes out higher than A, a hole is leaking or you have lifted a finger by mistake.

### Moving between them
The thumb and the index finger stay down for B, A and G. To go from B to A, add the middle finger. To go from A to G, add the ring finger. To climb back, lift one finger at a time. Do not take the whole hand off and replace it.

Practise this slow pattern: B A G, then G A B. Each note gets one gentle “doo”. Count four beats of rest before you repeat, so the class can hear the shape of the pattern.

### Order of pitch
From highest to lowest the three notes are B, A, G. From lowest to highest they are G, A, B. Saying the letter as you play helps the ear check the finger. If the letter in your mouth and the sound in the air disagree, stop and look at the fingers.

Use a chart or a video only to check the fingers, then look up again. Staring at the holes while you play makes the recorder droop and the seal break.

keyWords.meaning: the note played with thumb and the first two fingers of the left hand
the note played with thumb and the first three fingers of the left hand

examples.problem: How many front holes are covered for G?
steps: G uses holes 1, 2 and 3.
That is three front holes, plus the thumb at the back.

examples.problem: Put B, A and G in order from lowest to highest.
steps: Adding fingers lowers the note.
G has the most fingers covered, then A, then B.

activity.title: Step down and step up
steps: Play four A notes, then four G notes, checking the chart if needed.
Play B A G slowly, one “doo” each.
Play G A B slowly.
A partner watches whether the thumb stays down.
Rest, dry the mouthpiece, and try the pattern once more.

practice.question: Which fingers are down for note A?
practice.answer: Left thumb, index finger and middle finger.

practice.question: Which note is lower, A or G?
practice.answer: G

practice.question: Which finger do you add to change A into G?
practice.answer: The left ring finger.

summary: A is thumb plus two fingers. G is thumb plus three fingers.
The thumb stays down while you move between B, A and G.
G is the lowest of the three notes and B is the highest.

lessons.title: Simple melodies on B, A and G
objectives: Play a short melody using only B, A and G.
Keep the rhythm steady.
Breathe in places that do not break a short pattern.
lessons.intro: Three notes are enough for a real tune. A melody is simply notes in an order, played in time. Hot Cross Buns is the tune many beginners use because it needs nothing lower than G.
lessons.notes:
A melody is a tune: notes one after another with a rhythm. You already have the only notes this melody needs.

### Hot Cross Buns
Sing or say the rhythm first, then play.

B A G
B A G
G G G G
A A A A
B A G

Each letter in a group of three is one steady beat. In the lines of four letters, each letter is also one beat, so those lines feel busier because the same kind of beat is filled with repeated notes. Do not rush the four Gs or the four As.

### How to practise
1. Say the letter names in rhythm while you clap.
2. Finger the notes in silence, still saying the letters.
3. Play only the first line: B A G.
4. Add the second line.
5. Add the repeated Gs and As.
6. Play the whole melody once. Stop. Breathe. Play it again.

Breathe before you start and, if you need air, after a line, not in the middle of “B A G”. A short melody should feel like one sentence.

### Accuracy
Pitch accuracy means G sounds lower than A, and A sounds lower than B. Rhythm accuracy means the beats stay even. If the class plays together, one person can count “1 2 3” for the three-note lines. Counting is part of keeping the rhythm, just as it is in gymnastics.

When the first melody is secure, try this four-beat pattern of your own using only these notes: G A B A. Repeat it four times. You have now played both a known tune and a small pattern you can control.

keyWords.meaning: a tune made of notes in order
the steady pulse of the music

examples.problem: The line “G G G G” has one note name on each beat. How many G notes is that?
steps: Count the letters.
There are 4.

examples.problem: A player breathes between A and G in the first line, and the tune falls apart. Where is a better breath?
steps: Do not break the three-note group.
Breathe before the line or after it.
examples.answer: Before the line or after the whole “B A G”.

activity.title: Play Hot Cross Buns
materials: The letter pattern written on the board
steps: Clap and say the letters in rhythm.
Finger the melody in silence.
Play one line at a time.
Play the whole melody slowly with a partner, starting together.
If the pitch slips, stop and play B, A and G alone before you try the tune again.

practice.question: Which three notes does Hot Cross Buns use in this lesson?
practice.answer: B, A and G.

practice.question: Write the first two lines of the melody as note letters.
practice.answer: B A G / B A G

practice.question: What does rhythm accuracy mean here?
practice.answer: The beats stay even and the notes stay in time.

summary: Say and clap the rhythm before you play.
Hot Cross Buns uses B, A and G only.
Breathe between lines, and keep the beats even.

lessons.title: Playing together and giving feedback
objectives: Play a melody with a partner or a small group.
Comment on tone, fingering and rhythm kindly.
Show that you enjoy playing and that you care for the recorder afterwards.
lessons.intro: A tune played alone is practice. A tune played with others, and then talked about fairly, is a performance. You can enjoy the sound and still help someone improve.
lessons.notes:
Sit in a small group. Choose a leader to count “1, 2, ready, play”. Everyone starts on the same beat and plays Hot Cross Buns, or the pattern G A B A repeated. Listening is as important as blowing. If you cannot hear the group, you are too loud.

### What to watch and hear
- **Tone:** gentle and clear, or squeaky and forced?
- **Fingering:** did B, A and G sound in the right order, high to low?
- **Rhythm:** did the four repeated notes stay even?
- **Posture:** tall body, left hand on top, recorder slanting, no biting?
- **Care:** own instrument only, dry at the end?

### Feedback
Use two sentences.

- “I heard a clear tone on the Gs.”
- “Next time, keep the beats of the four As more even.”

Do not grab another person’s recorder to show them. Mime the fingers on your own. Accept feedback without arguing. Then play the melody once more, trying only the one change that was asked for.

### Enjoyment
The recorder is enjoyable when the tone is pleasant and the group starts together. That pleasure grows with short, regular practice, not with one long noisy session. When you finish, wipe the beak, shake out moisture, take the joints apart gently if that is your class routine, and store the recorder in its case. Thank the group. Playing well and looking after the instrument belong in the same lesson.

keyWords.meaning: a group playing together
comments that say what worked and what to improve

examples.problem: A group of 5 players each plays the melody twice. How many play-throughs does the group make in total?
steps: 5 players × 2 = 10

examples.problem: Someone says, “That was awful.” Rewrite it as useful feedback.
steps: Name one good point.
Give one next step.
examples.answer: Example: “I heard the B A G in the right order. Next time, soften the breath so the tone does not squeak.”

activity.title: Play, listen, improve
materials: Space to sit in groups of four
steps: The leader counts the group in and you play the melody together.
Listeners use the two-sentence feedback.
Play once more, changing only the point that was mentioned.
Swap so another learner leads.
Dry and store the recorders. Say one thing you enjoyed.

practice.question: What should a leader do before the group plays?
practice.answer: Count everyone in so they start together.

practice.question: Name two things you can comment on.
practice.answer: Any two: tone, fingering, rhythm, posture, care of the instrument.

practice.question: What do you do with the recorder at the end?
practice.answer: Wipe it, let the moisture out, and store it in its case.

summary: Start together and listen to the group.
Give one strength and one next step.
Enjoy the tune, then clean and store the recorder.

quiz.question: Which joint has the beak and the window?
quiz.explanation: The head joint is the top piece with the mouthpiece and the window.

quiz.question: Which hand goes nearer the beak?
options: Neither; the recorder is held in one fist
quiz.explanation: The left hand plays the upper holes for B, A and G.

quiz.question: Why must you not share a recorder mouthpiece?
quiz.answer: Germs can pass from one person to another and spread communicable diseases.

quiz.question: A plastic recorder should be washed in…
options: lukewarm soapy water, then rinsed and dried
quiz.explanation: Lukewarm water cleans it without warping it. It must be dried afterwards.

quiz.question: A good tone is produced by…
options: a gentle steady breath, tonguing, and sealed holes
covering the window with a finger
quiz.explanation: Gentle air, a clean tongue start and no leaks make a clear tone.

quiz.question: Note B is fingered with…
quiz.explanation: B uses the left thumb and the first front hole.

quiz.question: Which note is the lowest: B, A or G?
quiz.explanation: G uses the most fingers of the three and sounds the lowest.

quiz.question: Which pattern is the first line of Hot Cross Buns in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: The melody begins B A G, then repeats that pattern.

quiz.question: Where should you breathe in a short “B A G” line?
quiz.answer: Before the line or after it, not between the notes of the group.
quiz.explanation: A breath in the middle breaks the melody.

quiz.question: Which of these is useful feedback after a recorder performance?
options: “I heard a clear G. Next time, keep the four As more even.”
quiz.explanation: Feedback names a strength and one improvement.
